requirements.requirement: Run a long-running background worker as a managed systemd service named inventory-worker on node1
requirements.summary: A systemd unit file /etc/systemd/system/inventory-worker.service was created with a looping worker script, enabled and started via systemctl enable --now, confirmed active/enabled both before and after a full reboot cycle.

requirements.requirement: Service is confined so it writes only inside /var/lib/inventory
requirements.summary: Unit uses ProtectSystem=strict with ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/inventory plus PrivateTmp, ProtectHome, etc. Direct nsenter tests into the running process's mount namespace show a write to /etc fails (read-only filesystem) while a write to /var/lib/inventory succeeds, both pre- and post-reboot.
Unit sets NoNewPrivileges=yes; running process's /proc/<pid>/status shows NoNewPrivs: 1, confirmed both before and after the reboot.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol for node1 (pre-restart baseline, restart, boot identity change, recovery of service/data/sandboxing)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 34027437... with service active/enabled and 3 log lines. Reboot was acknowledged and the connection dropped and reconnected. Post-restart boot_id c2b754fb... differs from baseline and matches the fixed after_executor snapshot. Post-restart checks show the service auto-started, is still enabled/active, the inventory.log file preserved its pre-reboot lines and continued appending new ones, and both NoNewPrivs and the /etc-write-denied sandboxing behavior were re-verified.

overall_summary: The inventory-worker systemd service was deployed on node1 with a strong sandboxing profile (ProtectSystem=strict, ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/inventory, NoNewPrivileges=yes, plus numerous additional hardening directives), and confinement plus privilege restriction were directly verified via nsenter and /proc/<pid>/status checks. The mandated node1 restart protocol was also fully and coherently executed: a pre-reboot baseline, an acknowledged reboot with a boot identity change confirmed against the fixed lifecycle snapshots, and a post-reboot verification showing the service auto-started, its data file was preserved and continued appending, and both sandboxing controls remained intact. No unnecessary or unrestored mutations were found in the command trace.
limitations: The lifecycle 'after_prepare' phase is an alias of 'before_prepare' (prepare disabled), so preparer-vs-executor state separation relies entirely on the before_prepare vs after_executor diff, which is adequate here but reduces independent cross-validation depth.

Two reboot-window commands (cmd-01894796a0b84565, cmd-b855df29621e47be) returned connection errors, which is expected during a live reboot but means the exact moment of unavailability was not directly captured with a clean error state rather than transport-level exceptions.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map directly to task prerequisites (user/dir creation, worker script, unit file), bounded verification (nsenter write tests), or the mandated restart protocol. The one file written during a confinement test outside the approved unit config (/var/lib/inventory/should_succeed) was created purely to prove writability and was deleted immediately afterward in the next command; the failed /etc write attempts left no residue since they errored out. The post-reboot snapshot shows no failed services, package health remains consistent (manager=dnf), and new /tmp entries are only systemd-private per-service directories plus a small reboot.log, both expected artifacts of the sanctioned reboot rather than executor residue.
